Pure water freezes at 0 °C (32 °F), but when salt dissolves in the thin layer of water that is always present on or around ice, it forms a salt-water solution, or brine. In that solution, sodium and chloride ions get in the way of the orderly arrangement water molecules need to form ice crystals. As a result, the water can stay liquid at temperatures below 0 °C.

This is why spreading salt on a road can make existing ice or frost melt even when the surface is cold: the ice absorbs heat from the surroundings and turns into a concentrated brine rather than instantly refreezing. The more salt that is present, up to a practical limit, the lower the freezing point becomes.

That said, salt has limits. At very low temperatures, sodium chloride stops working well because the brine becomes too weak to prevent refreezing. In those conditions, road crews may use other de-icing chemicals or rely on sand for traction. So in everyday terms, road salt does not “warm up” the ice; it changes the physical properties of water by making it harder for ice crystals to form and survive. That simple chemical effect is what makes salting roads one of the most widely used methods for improving winter safety.

Airplanes fly because their wings generate lift. The simplest way to think about it is that the air moving over the top of the wing behaves differently from the air moving under it.

A wing is shaped so that air is forced to travel farther and usually faster over the curved upper surface than along the flatter lower surface. Because of that difference in airflow, the pressure above the wing becomes lower than the pressure below it. That pressure difference pushes the wing upward. That upward push is called lift.

Once the lift force is strong enough to overcome the airplane’s weight, the aircraft can rise off the ground and stay in the air. In practice, pilots also use the angle of the wing, speed, and throttle to control how much lift is produced.
